Triggers.value: Being in a locked or confined room
Being in a natural environment similar to where it happened

Threat.value: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger
Being superalert or watchful or on guard

Memory.value: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once
Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time
Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning

Negative Appraisals.value: I have lost my faith in people, life, or a higher power
My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe
I can't stop bad things from happening to me

issues.explanation: Threat items imply an ongoing personal-danger/being-followed formulation, which is hard to reconcile with trauma to a loved one; they read more like direct interpersonal victimization than fear for a loved one.

Within Threat, 'Checking Behind' and 'Avoid Unfamiliar Places' reflect hypervigilant danger avoidance, while 'Risky Behavior' points in the opposite direction behaviorally; this combination is possible but clinically strained without any other items supporting disinhibition.

Memory item 'Pain Recall' implies bodily re-experiencing of injury to the patient's own body, which is difficult to fit with trauma to a loved one unless she was also directly harmed; the other memory items do not suggest that.

issues.item: Threat: Risky Behavior: Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm
issues.explanation: For trauma to a loved one, a prominent risky-behavior item is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile, which is dominated by fear/avoidance and reliving rather than self-endangering behavior. It pulls the threat profile in a different direction without support from other nodes.

issues.item: Memory: Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event
issues.explanation: Pain recall in the same body parts as during the event implies the patient personally sustained bodily injury during the trauma. That is difficult to fit with trauma to a loved one, especially given no other items indicate direct physical victimization.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body
issues.explanation: The body-focused negative appraisals suggest distrust of one's own injured or trauma-reactive body, which fits direct bodily trauma better than trauma centered on harm to a loved one. In this profile they are not well supported by the trauma type or the other selected items.

issues.item: Triggers: Military Topics: Talks about military
issues.explanation: For trauma to a loved one, 'military topics' is hard to justify unless the loved one’s trauma was specifically military-related; that context is not represented anywhere else in the profile, so this trigger appears mismatched to the stated trauma type.

issues.item: Triggers: Locked Spaces: Being in a locked or confined room
issues.explanation: 'Locked spaces' suggests a confinement/entrapment trauma context, but the rest of the profile centers on reliving, terror, and generalized danger after trauma to a loved one rather than a personal entrapment event. Without corroborating memory or appraisal content, this trigger looks clinically out of place.

vignette:
# Leila

Leila was sixty-three when her younger brother Karim died in a hiking accident in the mountains of northern California. He had gone alone on a trail he thought he knew—a place of natural beauty he had visited twice before—and had slipped on loose rock near a ravine. His body was not found for three days. She learned about it over the phone while sitting at her desk at the accounting firm where she had worked for thirty-two years, and the sound of her supervisor's voice telling her that Karim was gone became, in her memory, indistinguishable from the sound of wind rushing through a canyon she had never seen.

In the weeks after his death, Leila could not sleep. She would lie awake at night, her heart racing without reason, her body drenched in sweat as though she herself were clinging to a rocky ledge in darkness. Her physician prescribed a mild sedative, but it did little good; the moment she began to drift, some internal alarm would jolt her awake—a phantom sensation of falling, of loose ground giving way beneath her. The sleep deprivation made her work suffer. She found herself unable to concentrate on the spreadsheets that had once been her refuge, numbers blurring on the screen. By autumn, six months after Karim's death, she had taken a leave of absence.

The triggers came without pattern or mercy. A locked conference room at work—the kind with no windows, where she and her team had once reviewed quarterly reports—became intolerable to her. The moment the door closed, her chest would tighten and she would feel certain that something terrible was about to happen, that she was trapped in a space from which escape was impossible. Being in any natural setting—even the small park near her apartment building with its trees and open sky—could transport her instantly back to the ravine, to the image of Karim's body crumpled on stone, though she had never actually seen it. A photograph of a hiking trail in a magazine, a friend's casual mention of a weekend getaway to the mountains, the face of someone who resembled her brother in profile—any of these could shatter her composure completely. When these moments struck, the memory would come back with such overwhelming sensory force that she could feel the wind on her skin, smell the earth and pine, hear the terrible silence that must have surrounded Karim in his final hours. The terror that accompanied these recollections was identical to the terror she had felt when first receiving the news, as though her nervous system had no capacity to distinguish between the event itself and the memory of it.

What frightened Leila most was her growing conviction that she could not prevent catastrophe, that her vigilance—however exhausting—was ultimately futile. She had come to believe that people were fundamentally untrustworthy, that the world was far more dangerous than she had ever allowed herself to acknowledge. This loss of faith in the basic safety of existence fed her hypervigilance; she monitored her surroundings obsessively, always searching for threats she could not name and could not adequately assess. When she tried to venture into unfamiliar places—a new grocery store, a different route to her apartment—her mind would race through scenarios of disaster. What if something happened and no one could reach her? What if she was trapped somewhere she did not know? The conviction that she was helpless, that bad things happened and she could do nothing to stop them, made it nearly impossible to leave her apartment. Her body seemed to have become her enemy; it reacted with panic to situations that rationally posed no danger, as though it possessed knowledge her conscious mind could not access. This bodily betrayal—the racing heart, the shortness of breath, the sense of impending doom that would grip her without warning—only deepened her sense that she could not trust her own perceptions, that safety was an illusion.

After nearly a year of isolation, barely able to work, her closest friend finally insisted she seek help. Leila sat in the waiting room of the trauma clinic, her hands trembling, terrified that acknowledging what had happened to her brother might somehow make it more real, yet knowing that the alternative—this suffocating prison of fear and avoidance—was no longer sustainable.
